topSignals.title: House passes the "Power for the People Act" (Ratepayer Protection Act) 417-3, forcing data centers to pay their own grid-upgrade costs — fuel cell stocks jump, then the Senate stalls it the next day.
topSignals.text: The bill defines "large load customers" (100 MW+ single-site peak demand) and directs state utility regulators to design rate structures so those customers — not ordinary ratepayers — bear the cost of new generation, transmission and distribution capacity built to serve them. Markets read this as tilting economics toward behind-the-meter power (SOFC's core value proposition): FuelCell Energy jumped 13% to $17.47, Plug Power climbed 7%, Bloom Energy rose 3% on the House vote (Sept 16). Progress then stalled on Sept 17 when Senate Energy and Natural Resources ranking member Martin Heinrich objected to a unanimous-consent request, so the bill is not law yet — the stock move prices in policy possibility, not an enacted mandate. Directly relevant to Dominic's business case: a codified cost-shift to data-center operators strengthens the argument for on-site/behind-the-meter SOFC over grid interconnection. Utility Dive | 24/7 Wall St. (stock reaction) | Roll Call (Senate stall)

lcoe.text: Power for the People Act (Top Signal #1): if enacted, would codify that 100 MW+ data-center loads bear the full cost of new grid generation/transmission/distribution built to serve them, rather than socializing it across ratepayers. This is a policy-side LCOE comparator, not a cost input directly — it raises the effective grid-power cost baseline that on-site SOFC needs to beat, strengthening SOFC's relative economics if enacted. Track Senate action; not yet law.

US ITC 48E confirmation: OBBBA-amended eligibility means natural-gas and biogas-fueled SOFC now qualify for the flat 30% ITC (construction start after Dec 31, 2025) without the previous zero-GHG-emissions test — material and likely underused in current LCOE capex assumptions if not already reflected. Domestic-content thresholds (45%/50%/55% in 2026/27/28) affect full-credit eligibility and should be checked against Elcogen/Topsoe/Bloom sourcing.

Carry-forward, unchanged: Henry Hub last independently confirmed at $2.81/MMBtu (Sept 9); EIA's Q3 2026 STEO forecast (dated, per Oct 2025 STEO) put Henry Hub around $3.91/MMBtu — a forecast, not a new spot print, and one to reconcile against the model's $4.00-4.30/MMBtu assumption; Virginia's $0.011/kWh self-generation tax; PJM's $555/MW-day backstop ceiling.
